extracted.intended_audience: aspiring/college-level creative writers (students, beginning nonfiction and fiction writers)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice on the drafting and revision process emphasizing permissive, uncensored first drafts followed by rigorous subsequent revisions (the 'down', 'up', and 'dental' drafts). Intended to help writers begin, gather material, and edit toward clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shitty first drafts are necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: All good writers write them. This is how they end up with good second drafts and terrific third drafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lamott's central claim: expect and accept that first drafts will be 'really, really shitty.' The passage rejects the fantasy of effortless, elegant first drafts and normalizes messy initial work as universal among successful writers. Anti-pattern: assuming first drafts must be polished or that some writers always produce perfect first drafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start by getting something — anything — down on paper (the down draft)
rubrics_metrics.description: Start somewhere. Start by getting something -- anything -- down on paper. The first draft is the down draft: you just get it down.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical rule: overcome inertia by producing raw material rather than aiming for finished wording. The 'down draft' is explicitly described as the phase where you simply put content on the page without trying to perfect it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write without self-censoring; let the childish/uncensored voice romp
rubrics_metrics.description: The first draft is the child's draft, where you let it all pour out and then let it romp all over the place, knowing that no one is going to see it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow characters and the narrator to say crude, sentimental, or over-the-top things (example: a character saying, 'Well, so what, Mr. Poopy Pants?'). This uncensored release can surface unexpected material or a single brilliant line that points the work's direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use successive, distinct revision phases: up draft and dental draft
rubrics_metrics.description: The second draft is the up draft — you fix it up. The third draft is the dental draft, where you check every tooth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framework for revision: 1) Down draft: get it out. 2) Up draft: clarify, say what you mean more accurately. 3) Dental draft: micro-editing — inspect sentences/words for loose, cramped, or decayed bits. Use these distinct aims to guide each pass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect and tolerate overly long, self-indulgent first drafts, then cut ruthlessly
rubrics_metrics.description: First drafts may be twice as long as they should be, with self-indulgent and boring beginnings and no ending; the next day go through it with a colored pen and take out everything you possibly can.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revision technique: deliberately allow the first draft to be expansive; on revision, remove excess material, find a new lead (maybe on page two), and craft a punchy ending. Lamott describes using a colored pen to excise material and restructure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trust the process; persist through panic and despair
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers often feel panic and despair ('I'm ruined... I'm toast'), but experience teaches one to trust the process 'sort of, more or less.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Behavioral guidance: when stuck, stop briefly (breathe, take breaks), resume, and remember that the awful first draft is part of the route to a good revision. Anti-pattern: quitting or catastrophizing at the first sign of difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use short assignments / break tasks into small parts ('bird by bird')
rubrics_metrics.description: Short assignments are helpful; 'bird by bird' — tackle pieces one at a time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pedagogical guideline: break writing into manageable chunks to reduce overwhelm and make steady progress. Lamott pairs this with the idea that small tasks and tolerating a bad first draft produce eventual clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gather raw material by observing and recording everything interesting
rubrics_metrics.description: When writing reviews she visited restaurants several times with opinionated friends and wrote down everything anyone said that was interesting or funny, then used notes later to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical method for reportage and descriptive writing: collect concrete details, dialogue, and funny/interesting lines during observation sessions; use these as source material when drafting. Example workflow: multiple visits, note-taking in situ, then composing from notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know that the first draft is private — use that privacy to be honest
rubrics_metrics.description: No one is going to see it, so you can let the voice go and be candid and messy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological permission: treating the first draft as confidential frees you from self-editing and increases the chance of discovering valuable material. Anti-pattern: prematurely sharing or judging the raw draft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit for focus and tone during revision (tone down overwrought parts, relocate lead, craft ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: During revision, find a new lead, tone down overwrought descriptions (e.g., 'it is just a piece of chicken'), remove misfitting quotes, and figure out a 'kicky place to end it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete revision goals: tighten focus, moderate voice where needed, ensure quotes/characters serve the piece, and create a satisfying ending. Lamott's own example: trimming food-review excesses and reworking structure to produce a publishable piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't idolize apparent effortless inspiration; accept struggle as normal
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'fantasy of the uninitiated' imagines writers who write fully formed passages; in reality, very few writers know what they're doing until they've done it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attitudinal guideline: avoid comparing your hidden process to others' finished work. Recognize that visible success often hides a messy drafting process; this reduces impostor feelings and unrealistic expectations.
